title: Metals and Non-metals
summary: Metals are malleable (beaten into sheets) and ductile (drawn into wires), have metallic lustre, are generally hard, are sonorous (ring when struck), have high density and are good conductors of heat and electricity; they are solids except mercury, a liquid. Non-metals are neither malleable nor ductile (brittle), have no lustre, are softer, non-sonorous, of low density and poor conductors; they may be solid (carbon, sulphur), liquid (bromine, the only liquid non-metal) or gas.

Exceptions: sodium and potassium are soft enough to cut with a knife; gallium melts on the palm; gold and silver are the most malleable and ductile metals; graphite and iodine have lustre; graphite is the only non-metal that conducts electricity; diamond, the hardest natural substance, conducts heat better than copper but not electricity. Gold, silver, platinum and copper occur free (native) in nature because they are unreactive. Gold is used for ornaments because it is lustrous, very malleable and ductile, and does not corrode.

Metals have 1, 2 or 3 valence electrons and lose them to form positive ions (cations) with a noble-gas configuration — Na (2,8,1) → Na⁺ (2,8); they are discharged at the cathode in electrolysis. Non-metals have 5, 6 or 7 valence electrons and gain electrons to form negative ions — Cl (2,8,7) + e⁻ → Cl⁻ (2,8,8).

With oxygen metals form oxides: 4Na + O₂ → 2Na₂O; 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO; 4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃. Metal oxides are basic (Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH; CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂), but Al₂O₃, ZnO, SnO and Fe₂O₃ are amphoteric — they react with both acids and bases (Al₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O; Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH → 2NaAlO₂ + H₂O).

With dilute acids metals give hydrogen: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂; Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂. With water: sodium and potassium react with cold water (2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂), magnesium with hot water, aluminium and iron only with steam, forming oxides (3Fe + 4H₂O → Fe₃O₄ + 4H₂). With bases: zinc and tin form zincate and stannate (Zn + 2NaOH → Na₂ZnO₂ + H₂).

Corrosion is the slow destruction of a metal surface by air and moisture; for iron it is called rusting. Rust is hydrated ferric oxide, Fe₂O₃·xH₂O, a flaky reddish-brown powder: 4Fe + 3O₂ + xH₂O → 2Fe₂O₃·xH₂O. Rusting needs both oxygen and moisture (a nail in boiled water under oil, or with anhydrous calcium chloride, does not rust). A green layer on old copper is basic copper carbonate. Prevention: painting; oiling and greasing; galvanisation (coating iron with zinc — galvanised sheets for roofs, buckets and drums, protected even when scratched because zinc corrodes first); alloying — iron with nickel and chromium gives stainless steel. Pure gold (24 carat) is too soft, so ornaments use 22-carat gold, an alloy.

A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its salt solution: Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu; Cu + 2AgNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2Ag (silver deposits on the copper and the solution turns blue); Ag + CuSO₄ → no reaction. Arranging metals in decreasing order of reactivity gives the activity (reactivity) series: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > [H] > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au.

Minerals are natural substances in the earth's crust that contain metals; an ore is a mineral from which a metal can be extracted profitably — every ore is a mineral but not every mineral is an ore. Metallurgy is the extraction of metals from ores: concentration of the ore, conversion to oxide, reduction to the metal, and refining. Low-reactivity metals: mercury from cinnabar (HgS) by heating alone — 2HgS + 3O₂ → 2HgO + 2SO₂; 2HgO → 2Hg + O₂. Medium-reactivity metals (zinc, iron, lead) occur as sulphides or carbonates, converted to oxides by roasting (heating sulphide ores in air: 2ZnS + 3O₂ → 2ZnO + 2SO₂) or calcination (heating carbonate ores in limited air: ZnCO₃ → ZnO + CO₂), then reduced with carbon (ZnO + C → Zn + CO). Thermite process: Fe₂O₃ + 2Al → 2Fe + Al₂O₃ — the heat gives molten iron for welding railway tracks; here Al is oxidised and acts as the reducing agent. Highly reactive metals (Na, K, Mg, Al) are obtained by electrolysis of their molten compounds (Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na at the cathode; Cl₂ at the anode).

Non-metals burn in oxygen to form oxides: S + O₂ → SO₂; C + O₂ → CO₂. Most non-metal oxides are acidic and dissolve in water to form acids — CO₂ + H₂O → H₂CO₃; SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄; N₂O₅ + H₂O → 2HNO₃ — and react with bases (CO₂ + 2NaOH → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O). Some are neutral — CO, N₂O (laughing gas), NO, H₂O. The oxides of nitrogen are N₂O and NO (neutral) and N₂O₃, NO₂, N₂O₄ and N₂O₅ (acidic). Halogens react with metals to form halides such as NaCl.

Metals: copper and aluminium for wires (ductile); iron, aluminium and stainless steel for utensils, machines and sheets; zinc, lead, mercury and lithium for cells; gold, silver and platinum for jewellery. Non-metals: hydrogen to make ammonia (for urea) and in fuels (water gas CO + H₂); silicon for chips and solar cells; phosphorus for phosphoric acid, fertilisers and matches; sulphur as a fungicide, in gunpowder and to make sulphuric acid, the 'king of chemicals'.

case.passage: Neha placed three clean iron nails in test tubes. Tube A had some tap water so that the nail was partly in water and partly in air. Tube B had boiled water covered by a layer of oil. Tube C was dry and contained anhydrous calcium chloride. After a week, only the nail in tube A was covered with a flaky reddish-brown substance. Her teacher said that the iron gate at home is painted, and buckets are made of galvanised iron, for the same reason.

vsa: State two properties of gold that make it suitable for making ornaments.
Gold is very malleable and ductile, so it can be shaped into fine designs, and it is lustrous and does not corrode or tarnish (unreactive).
What is galvanisation? Give one use.
Galvanisation is coating iron or steel with a thin layer of zinc to prevent rusting. Galvanised iron sheets are used for roofs, buckets, drums and trunks.
What is rust? Write two conditions necessary for rusting.
Rust is hydrated ferric oxide (Fe₂O₃·xH₂O), the reddish-brown flaky coating formed on iron. Rusting needs (1) oxygen (air) and (2) moisture (water).

or: Write balanced equations: (a) sodium burns in oxygen to give sodium oxide; (b) iron reacts with steam.

vsa: Write two ways to prevent rusting.
Any two: painting; oiling or greasing; galvanisation (zinc coating); alloying (stainless steel).

or: Name (a) a metal soft enough to cut with a knife and the hardest non-metal; (b) a metal and a non-metal that are liquid at room temperature.

vsa: What is the reactivity series? Arrange Cu, Fe, Na, Mg, Ag and Pb in decreasing order of reactivity.
The arrangement of metals in decreasing order of their reactivity is the reactivity (activity) series. Na > Mg > Fe > Pb > Cu > Ag.
A copper wire is dipped in silver nitrate solution. What will you observe? Write the reaction.
A shiny grey-white deposit of silver forms on the wire and the solution turns blue, because copper is more reactive than silver. Cu + 2AgNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2Ag.

or: Write the names and formulae of the oxides of nitrogen.
Nitrous oxide N₂O, nitric oxide NO, dinitrogen trioxide N₂O₃, nitrogen dioxide NO₂, dinitrogen tetroxide N₂O₄, dinitrogen pentoxide N₂O₅.

sa: What is the nature of non-metal oxides? Write the equation for the reaction of SO₃ with water.
Most non-metal oxides are acidic — they dissolve in water to form acids and react with bases to form salts and water (CO, N₂O and NO are neutral). SO₃ + H₂O → H₂SO₄ (sulphuric acid).

or: Name the ore of mercury and write the equations for the extraction of mercury from it.
Cinnabar (HgS). It is roasted: 2HgS + 3O₂ → 2HgO + 2SO₂; on further heating the oxide decomposes: 2HgO → 2Hg + O₂.

sa: What is the thermite process? Name the metal used, write the balanced equation and give one use.

In the thermite process aluminium powder reduces a metal oxide such as iron(III) oxide; the reaction gives so much heat that the iron formed is molten. Fe₂O₃ + 2Al → 2Fe + Al₂O₃. It is used to weld railway tracks and broken machine parts.
Zinc ores A and B give CO₂ and SO₂ respectively when heated. Identify A and B and write the steps, with equations, to obtain zinc from them.

A is zinc carbonate (calamine, ZnCO₃) and B is zinc sulphide (zinc blende, ZnS). Calcination of A: ZnCO₃ → ZnO + CO₂. Roasting of B: 2ZnS + 3O₂ → 2ZnO + 2SO₂. Reduction of the oxide with carbon: ZnO + C → Zn + CO.

sa.note: October 2022 also asked why metals are electropositive and non-metals electronegative — metals lose valence electrons to form positive ions; non-metals gain electrons to form negative ions.

sa: Write four chemical properties of metals with equations.

(1) With oxygen they form basic oxides: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO. (2) With water they form hydroxides or oxides and hydrogen: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂. (3) With dilute acids they give hydrogen: Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂. (4) A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from its salt: Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu.
A silver coin is put in copper sulphate solution and a copper coin in silver nitrate solution. What happens in each case and why?

Silver coin in CuSO₄: no reaction, because silver is less reactive than copper. Copper coin in AgNO₃: silver deposits on the coin and the solution turns blue, because copper is more reactive than silver and displaces it: Cu + 2AgNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2Ag.
la: Distinguish between metals and non-metals on the basis of five physical properties. Name a metal and a non-metal that are exceptions to any two of these.

Metals are malleable and ductile, non-metals brittle; metals have lustre, non-metals generally do not; metals are sonorous, non-metals not; metals are good conductors of heat and electricity, non-metals poor; metals are usually hard with high density, non-metals soft with low density. Exceptions: mercury is a liquid metal; sodium is a soft metal; graphite is a non-metal that conducts electricity; iodine and graphite are lustrous; diamond is a very hard non-metal.
What is corrosion? Describe an activity to show that both air and moisture are needed for rusting. Describe four methods of preventing rusting.

Corrosion is the slow destruction of a metal by the action of air and moisture; the rusting of iron forms Fe₂O₃·xH₂O. Activity: nail A in a test tube with some water (air and water), nail B in boiled water covered with oil (no air), nail C with anhydrous calcium chloride (no moisture); after a few days only nail A rusts. Prevention: (1) painting; (2) oiling and greasing; (3) galvanisation — coating with zinc; (4) alloying — stainless steel (iron with chromium and nickel).
How are metals of low, medium and high reactivity extracted from their ores? Give one example with equations for each.

Low reactivity — heating alone: cinnabar 2HgS + 3O₂ → 2HgO + 2SO₂; 2HgO → 2Hg + O₂. Medium reactivity — the sulphide or carbonate ore is roasted or calcined to the oxide and reduced with carbon: 2ZnS + 3O₂ → 2ZnO + 2SO₂; ZnCO₃ → ZnO + CO₂; ZnO + C → Zn + CO (or by aluminium in the thermite process). High reactivity — electrolysis of the molten compound: molten NaCl gives sodium at the cathode (Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na) and chlorine at the anode (2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻).
